scenes.title: The starting point
scenes.narration: Every few years a new video standard halves the bits needed for the same picture quality. VVC did that in 2020. The cost is computation: the VVC encoder is about ten times heavier than the HEVC encoder, and the decoder about twice. In a product, that computation has to be done in hardware.

scenes.title: What a codec does
scenes.narration: A codec predicts each block of the picture from what it has already coded, keeps only the difference, and applies a transform that concentrates that difference into a few coefficients. The small coefficients are then rounded away. The decoder reverses these steps, and the encoder contains a full decoder, so that both sides reconstruct the same picture.

scenes.title: The three tools
scenes.narration: VVC added two transforms, called MTS and LFNST, and a new in-loop filter called ALF. Each one saves a few percent of bit rate, which is significant in this field. They are small additions in the standard, but costly in hardware. My thesis covers these three tools, for the decoder and for the encoder.

scenes.title: Why a chip and not software
scenes.narration: Live video has a deadline for every frame. The company I worked with makes fanless encoders for vehicles and portable use, so software was not an option. A processor spends most of its energy moving instructions and data rather than computing. A chip designed for one task avoids that. The drawback is that a chip cannot be changed after manufacture, so the design has to be correct before it is made.

scenes.title: The throughput requirement
scenes.narration: 4K at sixty frames per second on a 450 megahertz chip means the transform must process four samples every clock cycle, for every block size. Every block must also take the same number of cycles, so that the following blocks never wait. Within that requirement, the goal was to make each block as small as possible in area, memory and power.

scenes.title: The transform
scenes.narration: The usual way to build a transform in hardware is to hard-wire its constants, and for HEVC that was the cheapest option. VVC has many more transform types and sizes, so I built both versions. The result was the opposite: sixty-four shared multipliers reading their coefficients from a small memory took sixty-three percent less silicon. The second transform, LFNST, was added in the same way. We did not find an earlier hardware implementation of LFNST in the literature.

scenes.title: ALF, the adaptive loop filter
scenes.narration: ALF is a seven by seven, diamond-shaped filter whose coefficients the encoder computes and transmits. Each four by four block is classified into one of twenty-five classes, and the kernel is rotated or flipped accordingly. Because the filter is symmetric, one engine with twenty-six multipliers handles luma, chroma, and the cross-component filter.

scenes.title: The memory problem
scenes.narration: To filter one block, ALF needs the eight blocks around it, so blocks have to wait in memory. Feeding the filter in the order Cr, Cb, then two luma blocks keeps the luma needed by the chroma filter already in the pipeline, and only two lines of blocks have to be stored. The memory is reduced by three quarters.

scenes.title: Results
scenes.narration: Every block runs at 450 megahertz on a 28 nanometre process with a fixed latency, and matches the reference software bit for bit. The blocks were integrated in the company's real-time encoder and decoder, and four papers came out of the work. One limitation: the encoder-side filter handles only luma and the largest blocks, because the full version did not fit the cycle budget.

scenes.title: The people
scenes.narration: Daniel Ménard and Olivier Déforges directed the thesis, and Wassim Hamidouche supervised the work day to day, at the IETR laboratory of INSA Rennes. The industrial partner provided the constraints and the chip the designs were integrated into. I defended the thesis in Rennes on the thirty-first of May, 2022.
